For typical virus and nanoparticle parameters, the depletion well reaches $2$-$6\,k_{\rm B}T$, capture times are $0.1$-$1\,{\rm ms}$, and the conditional success time is measurably shorter than the unconditional mean. Finite-volume and Chebyshev schemes reproduce the analytic results within their discretization errors and satisfy the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture prior to membrane wrapping and a reference for comparing crowding, near-wall mobility, and surface reactivity in endocytosis.

AI.tldr: A new stochastic theory for particle capture in crowded environments, incorporating exact depletion forces and near-wall mobility to model the transition from reaction-limited to diffusion-limited capture.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of thermodynamically consistent stochastic models for the pre-contact stage of viruses/nanoparticles approaching cell membranes in crowded extracellular environments.
AI.method: A thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory using exact Asakur-Oosawa depletion geometry, spatially varying near-wall mobility, and Robin radiation boundary conditions, solved via analytic quadrature and numerical Chebyshev schemes.
AI.result: Derived analytic solutions for mean reaction time, reaction-before-escape probability, and conditional success time, showing depletion wells of 2-6 kBT and capture times of 0.1-1 ms.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides a quantitative framework for understanding crowding-assisted particle capture before membrane wrapping, revealing that capture is a reaction-limited to diffusion-limited crossover process.

title: FACET: Feasibility-Automaton Complete Enumeration and Truncation-Free Scoring of Molecular Formulas from MS/MS
summary: Determining the neutral molecular formula of a precursor ion from its tandem mass (MS/MS) spectrum is the first step in identifying an unknown small molecule. Existing methods trade recall, whether the correct formula is among the candidates, against the cost of examining each candidate. Methods that examine each candidate in depth must first shorten the list, by limiting element counts or truncating it, and that is where the correct formula is lost. End-to-end regressors are fast but guarantee neither validity nor recall. We present FACET, which separates deciding which formulas to consider from deciding which one to choose. A feasibility automaton builds a formula one element count at a time and admits exactly the formulas that fit the precursor mass and satisfy the ring-and-double-bond and valence constraints. Run as an exhaustive search, it enumerates the complete feasible set, so every candidate is valid and recall is fixed by the chemical constraints rather than by a trained model. A small neural scoring head then ranks every feasible formula from one pass of a pretrained spectrum encoder, so no candidate is discarded. On the NPLIB1 benchmark FACET reaches top-1 accuracies of $0.859$ with the adduct known and $0.729$ with it unknown, compared with $0.766$ and $0.660$ for the strongest established method, and its recall is the highest. On the external CASMI 2022 set its recall is $1.000$, and with the adduct unknown it is the most accurate of the methods compared.

AI.tldr: FACET is a new method for determining neutral molecular formulas from MS/MS spectra that uses a feasibility automaton to ensure all chemically valid candidates are considered, followed by a neural scoring head to rank them, achieving superior accuracy and recall compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for molecular formula determination face a trade-off between recall and computational cost; shortening candidate lists often leads to losing the correct formula, while end-to-end regressors lack validity and recall guarantees.
AI.method: The paper proposes FACET, which separates formula selection from ranking. It uses a feasibility automaton to exhaustively enumerate all formulas that satisfy mass, valence, and ring-and-double-bond constraints, then applies a pretrained neural scoring head to rank the complete set of valid candidates.
AI.result: On the NPLIB1 benchmark, FACET achieved top-1 accuracies of 0.859 (adduct known) and 0.729 (adduct unknown), outperforming the strongest established methods. On the CASMI 2022 set, it achieved a recall of 1.000 and the highest accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FACET effectively solves the trade-off between recall and computational cost by ensuring a complete and chemically valid candidate set is evaluated, leading to state-of-the-art performance in molecular formula identification.

title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 AgenticLS Workshop; adds one experiment
summary: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **BioAgent-DF**, a framework designed to audit scientific AI agents by decoupling their decision-making (verdict) from the specific evidence (citations/data) they consume. It demonstrates that agents can reach the same conclusion using different data, and that restoring an agent's internal state can correct silent numerical errors in critical tasks like cardiac-safety assays.
AI.motivation: Scientific agents are prone to 'silent faults' where they provide consistent verdicts based on corrupted or inconsistent evidence. Current auditing often fails to distinguish between a wrong answer and the wrong evidence used to reach a correct answer.
AI.method:
The authors use **BioAgent-DF** to: 
1. **Isolate and Restore:** Capture evidence/values at specific computation sites and transplant them back to original coordinates to test agent repeatability.
2. **Compare Prompts:** Test baseline vs. explicit-example prompting to see if verdict instability can be mitigated.
3. **State Recovery:** Test whether replacing a prediction file vs. restoring the full execution state is more effective at correcting faulty decisions.
AI.result:
1. **Repeatability:** Models (Qwen3.5, Gemma 3) showed consistent shifts in citations when evidence changed.
2. **Recovery Success:** In a hERG cardiac-safety assay, restoring the execution state and certified scores recovered **100% (39/39)** of faulty decisions, whereas simply replacing the prediction file recovered **0%**.
3. **Efficiency:** A new streaming arithmetic check implementation improved execution/verification speed by **42.4%** compared to FP64 implementations without loss of accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Effective auditing of scientific AI must track **both** the evidence used and the final answer. Restoring the computational state is critical for rectifying errors caused by numerical faults.

title: Accurate automated photo-identification of Near Eastern and European fire salamanders
summary: Photo-identification underpins non-invasive capture-recapture monitoring of amphibians, but manual identification becomes slow and error-prone as reference libraries grow. Focusing on the Near Eastern fire salamander (Salamandra infraimmaculata), we developed a pipeline based on zero-shot local-feature matching (SuperPoint and LightGlue) without species-specific training and evaluated it on $2{,}440$ field photographs from Haifa and Tel Dan in northern Israel. We isolated the yellow spot pattern, scored image similarity by the number of high-confidence keypoint matches, which reduced a confound whereby many-spotted individuals accumulate spurious matches, and assigned identities across the database by two-tier clustering. Pipeline-assisted expert review corrected misidentifications, reducing the number of identities by almost a quarter. On held-out individuals, the pipeline ranked the correct individual first for $95.2\%$ of queries and recovered identities with an ARI of $0.958$. Without modification, it reached $95.1\%$ and $91.7\%$ top-1 accuracy on two datasets of the European fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) and recognised $93.7\%$ of recaptures in one of them, compared with $38$-$77\%$ for five established programs and $93.9\%$ for visual inspection. Zero-shot local-feature matching thus offers amphibian monitoring a re-identification tool that needs no training data, transfers between related species, scales to databases of over a thousand individuals, and can audit existing databases before capture-recapture analysis.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot photo-identification pipeline using SuperPoint and LightGlue for amphibian monitoring, achieving high accuracy across species without requiring species-specific training data.
AI.motivation: Manual photo-identification in amphibian capture-recapture monitoring is slow and error-prone as databases grow larger.
AI.method: A pipeline utilizing zero-shot local-feature matching (SuperPoint and LightGlue) to isolate yellow spot patterns, scoring similarity via high-confidence keypoint matches, and assigning identities through two-tier clustering.
AI.result: Achieved 95.2% top-1 accuracy for the Near Eastern fire salamander and high performance on European fire salamander datasets, outperforming established programs while maintaining accuracy comparable to visual inspection.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot local-feature matching is a scalable, transferable re-identification tool for amphibian monitoring that requires no training data and can audit existing databases.

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
comment: 54 pages, 6 figures, 24 tables. Preregistrations: this https URL (M4) and this https URL (M5). Primary category cs.LG: a test for learned action-conditioned models; cross-listed for the statistical method (stat.ME) and the biological application (q-bio.QM)
summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies two major methodological flaws in how researchers evaluate whether action-conditioned world models (AI models) actually learn causal relationships between actions and outcomes.
AI.motivation: Current diagnostic methods for world models—replacing/removing actions to measure accuracy loss—often yield false positives, leading researchers to believe a model has learned causality when it has actually just learned statistical correlations.
AI.method: The authors analyze model behavior under two specific failure modes: autocorrelated experimental designs and high-dimensional pooled data (e.g., pixel-based inputs). They propose using conditional randomization tests (e-values) to correct these errors.
AI.result:
1. **Autocorrelation Failure**: In non-randomized designs, models use future actions as proxies for unobserved historical states, creating a 'false effect.'
2. **Dimensionality Failure**: In pooled data (like video frames), small model errors are amplified by the number of pixels, creating overwhelming false evidence against the null hypothesis.
3. **Empirical Proof**: They demonstrate this by showing how a real-world optogenetic experiment was misinterpreted due to these statistical pitfalls.
AI.conclusion: To ensure validity, researchers must use conditional resampling that accounts for the full state of the experimental design and avoid unadjusted pooled scores in high-dimensional environments.

title: Comparative Strategies for Handling Imbalanced QSAR Regression: A Case Study on hERG Activity Prediction
summary: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. Data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies can have different effects on model performance. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. We also observed that different imbalance-handling strategies can have divergent effects depending on the model type. These findings highlight the importance of region-aware evaluation in regression QSAR modeling and provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate strategies for imbalanced datasets.

AI.tldr: Stop using global error metrics for QSAR regression; instead, evaluate models based on their accuracy within the specific target property ranges that matter most for practical applications.
AI.motivation: Standard regression evaluation often fails in QSAR because it treats sparse and dense data regions equally, whereas practical drug discovery often focuses on specific, high-interest property ranges (e.g., high potency).
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic comparison of data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies across two distinct model architectures: **Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN)** and **fingerprint-based machine learning models**.
AI.result: 1. **Metric Superiority**: Evaluating performance based on specific 'interest-regions' (defined by domain knowledge and distribution) provides a more reliable measure of utility than total region metrics. 2. **Model Sensitivity**: The effectiveness of imbalance-handling strategies is highly dependent on the model architecture (GCN vs. Fingerprints).
AI.conclusion: The paper addresses the critical but understudied problem of **data imbalance in regression-based QSAR modeling**, proposing a shift from global performance metrics to **region-aware evaluation**.

title: The (Butter)fly Dream: Linear Separability of World-Model Rollouts in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
summary: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error. Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.

AI.tldr: The study investigates whether a brain model (trained on a specific task) can distinguish between reality and a 'dream' (generative model simulations) better than an untrained model.
AI.motivation: Inspired by Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, the researchers ask if a neural network's internal representations contain 'signatures' of a simulated environment that are not present in pixel-level errors.
AI.method: An observer model (a fly visual system trained on optic-flow estimation) was presented with real video (MPI-Sintel) versus 'dreams' generated by three different world models (random walk, MDN-RNN, RSSM). A classifier (the judge) tested if the cell-type responses could distinguish reality from dreams.
AI.result: The trained observer significantly outperformed the untrained model and pixel-level statistics (AUC 0.85-0.99 vs. much lower). Notably, the model could even detect subtle temporal disturbances (swapped frames) that pixel-based methods could not, suggesting the brain model captures high-level temporal structure rather than just visual noise.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific training enables a neural network to detect the underlying 'defects' of a simulated world, effectively allowing the model to 'know' it is dreaming through its internal temporal processing.

title: Statistical mechanics of spontaneous behavior
summary: Why do a few behaviors fill most of an animal's time? The usual answer is that these behaviors are started more often, because learning and reinforcement favor them. Here we show that how long a behavior lasts can, by itself, explain much of what is observed. We consider a system that runs until it meets a constraint, such as a wall, and then resets. The fraction of time it spends in each behavior then follows the Boltzmann law, and the partition function is the mean time between resets. The four laws of thermodynamics follow as theorems from four postulates, and critical points that act as bottlenecks become the most occupied states. In 47 multi-day recordings of fruit flies, the dominant behavior accounts for only $13\%$ of bout starts yet fills $49\%$ of the time, and its typical duration identifies the individual fly. These results lay the groundwork for a statistical mechanics of behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that animal behavior patterns are driven by the duration of individual bouts rather than just the frequency of starting them, applying principles of statistical mechanics to explain behavioral dominance.
AI.motivation: To explain why a small number of specific behaviors occupy the majority of an animal's time, challenging the conventional view that this is solely due to learning and reinforcement.
AI.method: The authors model behavior as a system that runs until reaching a constraint and then resets, applying statistical mechanics and the Boltzmann law to analyze behavioral durations and partition functions.
AI.result: In fruit fly recordings, a dominant behavior accounted for only 13% of starts but 49% of total time, with its duration serving as a unique identifier for individual flies.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral patterns can be mathematically described using the laws of thermodynamics, establishing a foundation for a statistical mechanics of animal behavior.

title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
comment: 64 pages: 10-page main text with 4 figures and 1 table, plus references and a 49-page appendix with 15 figures and 25 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
summary: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that different virtual staining architectures prioritize either structural accuracy or phenotypic diversity, highlighting the need for multi-metric evaluation in cell biology.
AI.motivation: Current virtual staining models lack rigorous characterization regarding their performance on volumetric (3D) and temporal (time-lapse) data. Existing single-metric evaluations fail to capture the nuances required for diverse downstream biological tasks.
AI.method:
The authors developed a comprehensive evaluation suite consisting of: 
1. **Paired Datasets**: 3D time-lapse images with and without fluorescent labels.
2. **Baseline Models**: Regression-based and generative-based models.
3. **Three-Tier Metrics**: Measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation accuracy, and single-cell phenotype similarity.
AI.result:
The study reveals a critical **trade-off**: 
- **Regression models** excel at spatial localization (structural fidelity).
- **Generative models** excel at capturing phenotypic distributions (biological fidelity). 
This suggests that no single model is universally optimal for all biological applications.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces **DynaCell**, an evaluation framework specifically designed to benchmark 3D time-lapse virtual staining models for live-cell imaging.

title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
summary: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) rely on biological signals or shortcuts by using post-hoc attribution methods across cell-type annotation and perturbation prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Predictive performance metrics in scFMs do not reveal if models are making decisions based on biologically meaningful features or model-specific shortcuts.
AI.method: The authors apply post-hoc attribution to Cell2Sentence and scGPT for cell-type annotation, and to scGPT+STATE for perturbation prediction, comparing attribution patterns against marker genes and synthetic regulatory ground-truths.
AI.result: Attribution reveals how models use biological features, contextual interactions, and input pathways; it also shows that conclusions are highly sensitive to the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc attribution serves as a flexible diagnostic tool to understand scFM behavior, identify pitfalls, and inform future model development beyond standard performance metrics.

title: Prior Action Control Causally Alters Language-Model Plasticity
summary: Two copies of one language model start from identical weights and receive the same rewards during training. For one copy the rewards depend on its own answers. The other copy is yoked: it receives the first copy's rewards no matter what it answers, a design taken from the learned-helplessness experiments of animal learning. We ask whether the copy whose rewards depended on its answers, the copy with control, later learns a new task faster, that is, whether control changes the model's plasticity. In Experiment 1, copies of Qwen3-0.6B generated their own answers in a two-turn game and afterwards learned a new task. The copies with control learned the new task faster in every pair, and the advantage held on different starting models as well as on the larger Qwen3-1.7B. Copies with no reward signal, trained only on the updates that every copy shared, learned about as fast as the yoked copies. The advantage is therefore mostly a benefit of control, not damage from lacking it. Control had also changed how the copies answered, so the twins practiced different answers. That practice could carry part of the advantage, and Experiment 2 removed the difference. Both copies of a pair trained on the same answers, fixed in advance, in the same order, and received the same number of rewards. Only one copy's rewards followed the answers, and that copy again learned a new task faster. The advantage of the copies with control over their yoked twins could be forecast before the new task began from each copy's weights. In sum, control over rewards during earlier training left models faster at learning a new task later on, and a conventional model evaluation need not show it.

AI.tldr: The study investigates whether 'control' (the ability to influence one's own rewards) increases a language model's future plasticity (the ability to learn new tasks).
AI.motivation: Drawing from psychological 'learned helplessness' experiments, the researchers aimed to see if receiving rewards dependent on one's own actions (control) enhances subsequent learning capabilities compared to a 'yoked' version that receives rewards regardless of its actions.
AI.method: The researchers used two copies of the Qwen3 model (0.6B and 1.7B). One copy received rewards based on its own answers (Control), while the other received the same rewards regardless of its answers (Yoked/No-control).
AI.result: The 'Control' models learned a new subsequent task significantly faster than their 'Yoked' counterparts. This advantage was predictable based on the models' weights before the new task began.
AI.conclusion: Having agency/control over reward signals during training enhances a model's long-term plasticity. The benefit stems from the presence of control rather than the damage caused by its absence. Furthermore, standard evaluations may fail to detect this enhanced learning capacity.

title: A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines
comment: 44 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track)
summary: MRI morphometry pipelines are often evaluated by measurement agreement or downstream accuracy, yet their scientific value depends on the conclusions they support. Two pipelines can produce similar feature-level results yet support different conclusions about aging, cognitive decline, or neurodegeneration. We introduce Scientific Claim Stability (SCS), a claim-centric evaluation framework that converts region-of-interest (ROI) morphometry tables into auditable claim cards and evaluates their support under changes in dataset, processing pipeline, atlas, feature family, and target. Across 10,370 MRI scans from three datasets and five cohorts, SCS generates 2,783 claim cards and evaluates 89 claim-family pairs. The evaluation distinguishes stable, transferable, and fragile claims. FreeSurfer 8-FastSurfer comparisons show high evidence concordance and low anatomical-support overlap under the primary covariate specification. Acquisition-adjusted analyses show that the magnitude of support disagreement depends on the model specification. Structured review by specialists in geriatrics, neuroscience, and radiology, alongside auxiliary ChatGPT and Gemini reviewers, assesses claim plausibility, clarity, faithfulness, usefulness, and caution. SCS provides a reproducible way to audit the evidential stability of morphometry claims without assuming a universal gold standard.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **Scientific Claim Stability (SCS)**, a new evaluation framework that shifts the focus of MRI morphometry assessment from raw data accuracy to the stability of the scientific conclusions (claims) derived from that data.
AI.motivation: Current MRI pipelines are typically evaluated by how well they match a 'gold standard' or their statistical agreement. However, two pipelines with similar statistical outputs can lead to contradictory scientific conclusions regarding neurodegeneration or aging.
AI.method:
1. **Claim Card Generation:** Converts ROI morphometry tables into auditable claim cards.
2. **Stress Testing:** Evaluates claim stability across variations in datasets, processing pipelines (e.g., FreeSurfer vs. FastSurfer), atlases, and covariates.
3. **Classification:** Categorizes claims into **Stable**, **Transferable**, or **Fragile**.
4. **Multi-modal Review:** Uses human specialists (geriatrics, neuroscience, radiology) and LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini) to assess claim quality (plausibility, faithfulness, etc.).
AI.result: The framework successfully audited 2,783 claim cards across 10,370 scans. It revealed that while pipeline concordance may be high, anatomical support often overlaps poorly, and the stability of a claim is heavily dependent on the statistical model specification.
AI.conclusion: SCS provides a reproducible, 'gold-standard-free' method to audit whether scientific findings in neuroimaging are robust or merely artifacts of specific processing choices.

title: Substrate hypergraph cycles: unique steady states and persistence for every enzyme assignment; oscillations enabled by enzyme sharing
summary: We associate a directed substrate hypergraph with an enzymatic reaction system. The hypergraph records which substrates each composite reaction consumes and produces, and each composite reaction is realized by a Henri--Michaelis--Menten (HMM) module whose enzyme may be distinct, shared with other reactions, or absent. We call the hypergraph a cycle when it is strongly connected and every substrate is produced by exactly one reaction and consumed by exactly one reaction, each time with coefficient one; equivalently, its dual is a strongly connected ordinary directed graph. For a cycle, every HMM realization, under every enzyme assignment and for all positive rate constants, has exactly one positive steady state in each stoichiometric compatibility class that contains a strictly positive point, and no steady state on the boundary of such a class, and every trajectory in such a class is persistent. The interior dynamics, in contrast, depend on how enzymes are shared. When each enzyme catalyzes at most one reaction, every trajectory in such a class converges to its unique steady state. With enzyme sharing, convergence can fail even for the three-substrate transformation cycle $X_1\to X_2\to X_3\to X_1$: if two transformations share an enzyme and the third has its own enzyme or none, the steady state can undergo a supercritical Hopf bifurcation that produces a stable limit cycle. Thus the substrate structure controls existence, uniqueness, and persistence, while the pattern of enzyme sharing controls the interior dynamics. The results extend to weighted cycles, which allow higher stoichiometric coefficients, and to longer chains of intermediates.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how the structural organization of enzymatic reaction systems (modeled as directed substrate hypergraphs) dictates their dynamical behavior, specifically distinguishing between substrate structure and enzyme distribution.
AI.motivation: To understand how the topology of reactions (what is consumed/produced) and the allocation of enzymes (which reaction uses which enzyme) jointly influence the stability and existence of steady states in biochemical networks.
AI.method: The authors utilize a mathematical framework of **directed substrate hypergraphs** where reactions are modeled as **Henri-Michaelis-Menten (HMM) modules**. They define a specific topology called a **'cycle'** to analyze existence, uniqueness, and persistence.
AI.result: The study identifies a critical decoupling between two structural components:
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that **substrate structure** (the hypergraph cycle) guarantees existence, uniqueness, and persistence of steady states, while **enzyme sharing patterns** determine the interior dynamics (e.g., whether the system converges to a steady state or enters a stable limit cycle via Hopf bifurcation).

title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding
comment: This is the camera-ready version accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Abstract shortened to respect the arXiv limit of 1920 characters. Please see the PDF for the full abstract
summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.

AI.tldr: AVID is a new 5.0T fMRI dataset using auditory cues to provide a cleaner, large-scale resource for decoding brain-generated visual imagery without visual interference.
AI.motivation: Current VMI research suffers from: 1) lack of training-scale data; 2) sensory contamination (visual/memory confounds); and 3) poor control over fine-grained visual attributes.
AI.method: The authors utilize **auditory-induced VMI** (using spoken descriptions) to eliminate visual/mnemonic confounds found in traditional visual-prompt paradigms. The dataset features **67 hours of 5.0T fMRI recordings** from nine participants, organized into two tracks: a complex **scene-level split** (naturalistic Mandarin) and a controlled **simple split** (explicit visual attributes). They also propose a new evaluation protocol that separates **semantic alignment** from **source-image consistency**.
AI.result: Baseline testing shows current reconstruction models struggle with AVID but can successfully capture **high-level scene semantics** from auditory descriptions. AVID serves as both a training foundation and a benchmark for pure endogenous imagery decoding.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces **AVID**, a novel, large-scale fMRI dataset designed to advance Visual Mental Imagery (VMI) decoding by addressing critical flaws in existing datasets.

title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
comment: Presented at 3rd Workshop on Multi-modal Foundation Models and Large Language Models for Life Sciences (ICML 2026)
summary: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **HistoTx**, an early-fusion vision transformer architecture designed to integrate spatial transcriptomics with whole slide images (WSIs) for more holistic tissue analysis.
AI.motivation: Current ML methods for multimodal tissue analysis use transcriptomics only as a training signal (supervised/contrastive learning). This makes inference purely image-driven, failing to leverage molecular data as a functional input modality during inference.
AI.method:
1. **Early-Fusion Architecture**: Constructs transcript tokens at arbitrary resolutions and merges them with image patch tokens.
2. **Joint Processing**: Uses a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction.
3. **Training Strategy**: Performs self-supervised pretraining by continuing from a pretrained pathology foundation model using paired image-transcriptomics data.
AI.result:
1. **Image-only Inference**: Maintains baseline performance while improving tasks requiring molecular context (e.g., gene expression prediction).
2. **Multimodal Inference**: When both image and transcript data are provided, the model outperforms unimodal approaches.
AI.conclusion: By treating transcriptomics as a first-class input rather than just a supervision signal, HistoTx achieves superior cross-modal synergy.

title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Code available at: this https URL
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the AI-FAIR metadata framework and an agentic evaluation workflow to create a bidirectional data-model loop, ensuring AI-driven insights are returned to data collectors.
AI.motivation: AI adoption in ecology is hindered by fragmented data infrastructure and a unidirectional value flow where derived insights (like annotations) fail to return to the original data collectors.
AI.method: Proposed an extension of FAIR principles called AI-FAIR metadata criteria based on a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle, accompanied by an agentic evaluation workflow for assessing dataset readiness.
AI.result: A modular, reusable assessment tool and a domain-appropriate checklist that evaluates machine-learning readiness, traceability, and ethical stewardship.
AI.conclusion: The AI-FAIR framework aims to close the loop between models and data, ensuring AI-enabled science enriches the original datasets to foster further scientific discovery.

title: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets
comment: Accepted at the AI for Drug Discovery workshop --- NeurIPS 2026
summary: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context. Using an intersection-over-union objective and evaluation metric (range-IoU), RangeFinder achieves a range-IoU of $0.464 \pm 0.002$, outperforming all deployable baselines while requiring only $12.2$ ms per pocket. We also quantify our method's ability to reduce the ligand search space while retaining compatible binders; in this regard, RangeFinder achieves a Reduction-Recall F-Score of $0.543 \pm 0.011$ --- once again outperforming all deployable baselines. Ablation experiments indicate that RangeFinder's performance depends more strongly on the density and quality of ligand supervision than on any individual input modality or specialized training strategy. Together, these results position RangeFinder as an inexpensive and effective molecular filtering prior, with demonstrated potential in narrowing the ligand search space of target pockets before docking, generation, or synthesis. The code for this project can be found at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: RangeFinder is an SE(3)-equivariant transformer model that predicts physicochemical property ranges for protein pockets to efficiently filter the ligand search space.
AI.motivation: Current ML approaches for ligand identification focus on generating candidates or scoring pairs, but fail to provide information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket.
AI.method: RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model trained on BioLiP2 data, which predicts ranges for nine physicochemical properties using an intersection-over-union (IoU) objective.
AI.result: Achieved a range-IoU of 0.464 and a Reduction-Recall F-Score of 0.543, outperforming all deployable baselines with a fast inference time of 12.2 ms per pocket.
AI.conclusion: RangeFinder is an effective and inexpensive molecular filtering prior that can significantly narrow the ligand search space before subsequent docking, generation, or synthesis steps.

title: In-depth data movement characterization of DNA read mapping algorithms
summary: Read mapping algorithms represent a critical bottleneck in genomic analysis pipelines due to the resources required; a problem that is becoming more pronounced as sequencing technologies advance and datasets expand. We present an extensive workload characterization of leading read mapping algorithms across diverse sequencing technologies to identify hardware acceleration and optimization opportunities. We analyzed the following implementations: MashMap, wfmash, and Minimap2 for whole-genome alignment (WGA); NGMLR, Minimap2, and LRA for long reads; and Bowtie2, BWA-MEM, StrobeAlign, and minibwa for short reads. We used the Intel VTune Profiler for detailed memory analysis to identify memory- bound functions, cache usage patterns, and data transfer bottlenecks. We further analyzed a selected subset of alignment tools using the DAMOV-SIM simulator to obtain a more granular view of data movement characteristics for two different cache structures. Based on our results, Minimap2 emerges as the fastest alignment tool for long read scenarios, but falls behind in whole-genome alignment due to poor multithreading. Across all three categories, some programs (e.g., LRA, BWA-MEM) are highly memory-bound. More in-depth analysis via DAMOV-SIM revealed that some memory-bound tools, in particular, do not fully utilize the multi-level cache hierarchy in modern multi-core CPU architectures. Our results show that while some tools require algorithmic redesign for performance gains, some others can benefit from running on PIM architectures.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive workload characterization of various read mapping algorithms reveals significant memory-bound bottlenecks and cache underutilization, suggesting opportunities for algorithmic redesign or PIM acceleration.
AI.motivation: Read mapping is a critical bottleneck in genomic pipelines due to increasing sequencing data volumes and high resource requirements.
AI.method: Workload characterization of leading read mapping algorithms using Intel VTune Profiler for memory analysis and DAMOV-SIM simulator for granular data movement and cache hierarchy analysis.
AI.result: Minimap2 is fastest for long reads but suboptimal for WGA due to poor multithreading; many tools (LRA, BWA-MEM) are highly memory-bound and fail to fully utilize modern multi-level cache hierarchies.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies that some mapping tools require algorithmic redesign for better performance, while others, particularly those highly memory-bound, are strong candidates for Processing-In-Memory (PIM) architectures.

title: Can AI Do Formal Demography? Why Vaccinating the Oldest Saves Both the Most Lives and the Most Years of Life
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure
summary: Can AI contribute to formal demography? We report an experiment in which an AI model, Claude, was asked to explain and then simplify the proof of an earlier result: that vaccinating the oldest against COVID-19 saves both the most lives and the most years of life, because the years saved per person treated rise with age. The model proposed a new proof that is shorter, more intuitive, and somewhat more general than the original, built from a known life-table identity and the definition of convexity. It states the condition for the result as the convexity of the reciprocal of the hazard, which can be checked from the hazard alone and holds for most familiar parametric models, and it yields a lower bound on life expectancy whenever that condition is met. Prompted by a further question, the model also gave an exact form of the condition, showing how far convexity can be relaxed. The model traced these identities and related results in earlier literature. An edited record of the sessions is provided, and complete transcripts are available on request. The exercise suggests that AI can revisit established results, make them easier to understand, and prove valuable generalizations.

AI.tldr: The paper explores whether AI can contribute to formal demography by using Claude to refine and generalize an existing mathematical proof regarding COVID-19 vaccination strategies.
AI.motivation: To test if Large Language Models (LLMs) can go beyond mere text generation to perform mathematical reasoning, simplification, and generalization of established demographic theories.
AI.method: The researchers conducted an experiment where an AI model (Claude) was tasked with explaining, simplifying, and extending a known proof: that vaccinating the oldest saves the most lives/years due to age-related scaling.
AI.result:
The AI successfully: 
1. Developed a shorter, more intuitive proof using life-table identities and convexity.
2. Identified a specific condition (convexity of the reciprocal of the hazard) that generalizes the result.
3. Provided a lower bound for life expectancy based on this condition.
4. Traced the mathematical identities back to existing literature.
AI.conclusion: AI demonstrates potential as a collaborative tool in formal sciences, capable of revisiting established results, simplifying complex proofs, and discovering useful mathematical generalizations.
